detail.longDescription: I'm invoking a CLI tool from Python using: import subprocess, shlex cmd = f'somecli eval {shlex.quote(js_code)}' subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, capture_output=True, text=True) This works correctly on Linux/macOS, but on Windows the argument (containing characters like < , > , && , => , backticks) gets mangled — the target CLI reports things like "SyntaxError: Invalid or unexpected token", even though the exact same command string is correct POSIX shell syntax. I understand shell=True on Windows invokes cmd.exe instead of /bin/sh , and shlex.quote() only produces POSIX-safe quoting. What's the correct, portable way to pass a single arbitrary string argument (containing shell metacharacters) to a subprocess so it survives on both platforms? The fix I ended up using was avoiding the shell entirely — resolving the tool's real executable and calling it via an argv list with shell=False : subprocess.run([resolved_exe, entry_script, *args], shell=False, ...) Is this the recommended approach, or is there a cleaner cross-platform way to keep using shell=True safely?
